    #32670. Five major challenges that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2662 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Five major challenges that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • In a recent development, but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • Recent findings suggest that before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    In a recent development, but despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile problems as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    Recent findings suggest that before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    Litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    According to recent reports, after a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the problem, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    It has been revealed that once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court announces in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    Sources indicate that the court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    Recent findings suggest that for a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely reveals that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    Industry observers note that once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile issues that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    One week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    According to recent reports, this ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    Shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either at the moment serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    In a recent development, in March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    Sources indicate that U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    On Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    As expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    In a recent development, this week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    In a recent development, nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    Last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the issue will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    It has been revealed that in addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    In a recent development, in a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    Sources indicate that because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    As I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration problems dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    And there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    It has been revealed that suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    The responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    The rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    Recent findings suggest that several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are right now considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, New Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the company. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    The responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    According to recent reports, in its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to glitch universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    Sources indicate that after CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    Industry observers note that the case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    That deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    The justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #32666. Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify.
    • It has been revealed that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton stated the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

    It has been revealed that some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

    It has been revealed that it is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

    So how can one tell the difference?

    Industry observers note that as we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

    Political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

    The 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each upcoming circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

    But circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

    It has been revealed that timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

    To clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This indicates, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

    Finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

    The allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”.

    Jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    #32664. Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (603 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, originally published on Nov.
    • Industry observers note that the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon.
    • Sources indicate that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

    Industry observers note that the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”.

    Sources indicate that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he revealed that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

    After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, revealed her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

    In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

    When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

    Sources indicate that on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it concerns a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 20, 2026, 11:10 am CST.

    In a recent development, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that newly introduced candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

    According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both remarked they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that upcoming candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

    “Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”.

    “A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

    Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

    “The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s key to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

    Industry observers note that smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

    In a recent development, “We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”.

    Sources indicate that after adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a upcoming lower-court ruling.

    Finally, a few housekeeping notes:.

    On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

    Industry observers note that also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

    On Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

    On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such complications as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

    Sources indicate that the December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Michael Phillis, Associated Press.

    In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”.

    It has been revealed that on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the Upcoming York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”.

    Nicholas Kristof, The Latest York Times.

    Industry observers note that in a column for The New York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

    Recent findings suggest that in a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

    According to recent reports, in a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” stated Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”.

    On Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Sources indicate that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

    By Jordan J. Ballor & Logan Tantibanchachai.

    In a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan J. Ballor and Logan Tantibanchachai reflected on Democrats’ recent embrace of court packing, which they “define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.” Such an approach to court reform “risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently,” they wrote.

    By César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández.

    Recent findings suggest that in his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored what Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could mean for a challenge to an Iowa law criminalizing certain immigration-related conduct, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Because Iowa’s Republican attorney general lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, it’s now unclear if the state will move forward with its defense of the law, “providing yet another reason why elections matter.”.

    In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky revisited the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, during which several conservative justices appeared to suggest “that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.” Such an approach to free exercise would be at odds “with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact ... is not enough to prove discrimination,” Chemerinsky contended.

    In a recent development, in her In the Interim column on Monday, Taraleigh Davis revisited comments made by Justice Samuel Alito this fall about the court’s emergency docket, including why it’s so busy these days. The data, according to Davis, “support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sarah Isgur and David French discuss the nature of lame-duck confirmations after the showdown between Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, journalists’ records, and weakening the presidential veto.

    Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka continue their discussion on the significance of and fallout from this month’s midterm elections.

    Industry observers note that the Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

    Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two New Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

    Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, Newly introduced Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

    According to recent reports, woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He promptly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

    During the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” Latest Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

    Recent findings suggest that in 1823, the Latest Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

    Sources indicate that in 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

    Sources indicate that in 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of Fresh Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

    In 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”.

    Sources indicate that in 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of Latest York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

    Recent findings suggest that woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun stated – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

    Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, Newly introduced Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

    MR. MILLER: “– No, I think they mean what a district judge honoring his Article III commission concludes after an intensive evaluation of the entirety of the complaint, looking for that strong inference, putting on his sort of motion to dismiss 12(b)(6) hat, states okay –”.

    CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “Just okay?”.

    MR. MILLER: “– No, I did not mean that. Don't take me literally on that. For heavens sakes, I'm from Brooklyn. I'm very colloquial. I'm very sorry about that.”.

    In a recent development, JUSTICE SCALIA: “Let me write that down. We should not take you literally. All right.”.

    Even justices have regrets

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (171 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.
    • But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement.
    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a newly introduced estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    According to recent reports, recommended Citation: Nora Collins, Even justices have regrets, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/even-justices-have-regrets/.

    Senior Forward Deployed Engineer at Clutch

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions.
    • As a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent.
    • In a recent development, this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that clutch builds AI agents that work on behalf of credit unions. Emma, our collections agent, is live at five credit unions and handled 60,000+ member conversations in her first twelve weeks at one of them. Behind her is a growing portfolio: origination, fraud step-up, member (re)engagement and activation agents, all built on the same Agents Platform (TypeScript, NestJS, our own agent SDK, MCP, Temporal, promptfoo).

    As a FDE you are one of the two engineers on an agent. You take it from "sold" to "live and performing" at a specific credit union: you sit in the discovery sessions, you build the integrations to their core banking and loan systems, you author and tune the agent's behavior, you run the live tests with their staff, and you stay with it through go-live and the first weeks of production. When something needs a person in the room, you are the one who flies.

    In a recent development, this is a senior engineering role, not a solutions or support role. You write production code in our monorepo every week: integrations, modules, and the agents themselves (prompts, tools, evals), together with the other engineers on the pod. The difference from a traditional engineer is that you are on site more often, you make judgment calls in front of the customer, and you own the outcome. What you learn in the field flows straight back into the product: defaults, playbooks, and the platform capabilities the next agent will need.

    Sources indicate that you build; our AI Operations Managers deliver. The pod (pod lead plus engineers) designs and builds each agent in a high-touch way with the first customers. Once the agent is defined and live, AI Ops coordinates the implementations, configuration and ongoing success at the next credit unions. You hand them something that works and a playbook to run it.

    This role requires roughly 20% of travel on average, with one- to two-week stretches around kickoffs and go-lives. Based in the US, able to travel on short notice.

    Industry observers note that you'll join the Agents team, a small, senior group operating as a startup inside Clutch: seven engineers, a dedicated AI product group, and AI sales specialists, working directly with some of the largest credit unions in the country. Every agent is staffed by a pair of engineers, one leaning toward the conversation and LLM side, one toward software and integrations, with a pod lead who owns the product day to day. There is no layer between you and the customer, and no layer between you and the platform team.

    The operating style is direct, written, and evidence-driven: BLUF updates, evals over opinions, business outcomes over ticket counts. The team is spread across Brazil, Argentina and the US and works async by default. Being on site is a tool we use at specific moments (kickoff, live testing, go-live), not a permanent posting.

    Ship your first production change to a live agent through the team's review process, and be able to explain how a member's call flows through the Agents Platform end to end.

    Learn one agent deeply: system prompt, tool contracts, orchestration triggers, compliance gates, and the implementation process from kickoff to go-live.

    Join at least one credit union implementation as the second engineer, including a live testing session with their staff.

    Map where the current implementation process loses time and where a default or a tool would have removed a round trip.

    Own the technical side of one credit union implementation end to end: core and LOS integration, agent configuration, testing, go-live, and the first weeks of production.

    Run the eval and tuning loop for your agent (golden transcripts, rubric judges, regression suite) and be trusted to change its behavior without a second engineer checking your work.

    Have completed at least two on-site visits and turned what you heard there into product decisions with your pod lead and PM.

    Contribute at least one reusable capability back to the Agents Platform that the next implementation will not have to rebuild.

    Have taken one net-new agent from sold to live at its first credit union, with data you can show the partner.

    Be the engineer credit union staff ask for by name when something in their deployment needs to change.

    Have written the implementation playbook for your agent well enough that the AI Ops team runs the second and third credit union without you.

    Be shaping what the next agents look like, because you have seen where the current ones break in the field.

    In a recent development, 7+ years of software engineering in a fast-paced environment, preferably in SaaS and/or Fintech, with senior TypeScript and Node.js backend experience in a large codebase (NestJS, CQRS, schema-validated boundaries, dependency injection). We do not count years of AI experience; the field is too young for that to mean anything. We look at what you have shipped and how you reason about it.

    Integration and API engineering: secure service-to-service endpoints, third-party APIs, webhooks, and the patience to work with legacy banking systems that were not designed to be integrated.

    Sources indicate that security and auth judgment: OAuth and machine-to-machine auth, tenant-scoped access, secrets handling, no PII in logs. Our agents touch sensitive member data and operate under consumer-contact regulation.

    Sources indicate that customer presence: you can sit across from a VP of Collections, hear a request, and say "here is what I recommend and why", including when the answer is no. You are comfortable making calls in the room and owning them afterwards.

    Code-quality judgment under deadline pressure: you take on debt deliberately, name it, and pay it down, rather than gold-plating or leaving silent debt behind.

    Recent findings suggest that genuine appetite for LLM agents: eval discipline for non-deterministic systems, reading a system prompt like code, understanding that some decisions must never reach the model. Curiosity plus shipped work is enough; research depth is not required.

    Nice to have, explicitly not required: voice and telephony (LiveKit, Twilio), Temporal or event-driven orchestration, Python, core banking or LOS integration experience, credit union or banking domain knowledge.

    Remote Flexibility: Enjoy the freedom of remote work from anywhere, balancing life and career seamlessly.

    Unforgettable Off-Sites: Twice a year, bond with colleagues in exciting destinations, fostering teamwork and fresh ideas.

    Paid Time Off: Enjoy flexible PTO days yearly for relaxation and rejuvenation.

    Stock Options: Joining us means having a stake in our success, so you'll receive stock options as part of your compensation package.

    Home Office Setup: Create your ideal workspace with a dedicated budget for home office essentials.

    Work Trip Budget: Grow personally and professionally with a budget for work-related trips and co-working.

    Health Coverage: Prioritize your well-being with comprehensive health and dental insurance intends.

    Clutch is a revolutionary vertical SaaS tech giant, proudly backed by Andreessen Horowitz (A16z), aimed at revolutionizing the way Credit Unions engage and change the lives of their members. As a champion of financial well-being, we address the urgent need for affordable lending solutions in an era where the average American grapples with over $155,000 in household debt. Unlike traditional financial institutions, Clutch develops software to turn Credit Unions into FinTech lenders and leverage their balance sheets to responsibly lend to over 130M Americans. Our mission extends beyond mere financial transactions; we strive to fundamentally enhance the way credit unions interact with their members. By integrating cutting-edge technologies and user-centric designs, we help credit unions provide seamless digital experiences that are on par with leading tech companies. This approach not only preserves but revitalizes the longstanding tradition of community and member-focused service inherent to credit unions.

    Recent findings suggest that clutch is an equal opportunity employer. All applicants will be considered for employment without attention to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin, veteran or disability status.

Base salary does not include bonus, equity, or benefits, which are offered in addition as applicable.Applications will be accepted on an ongoing basis.

    Our organization participates in E-Verify. Click here to learn about E-Verify.A Note About AI at ClutchWe love AI. We use it often and encourage our team to creatively and effectively leverage AI tools in their work. If you join Clutch, we hope you'll bring the same enthusiasm for exploring how AI can amplify impact, productivity, and innovation.That noted, during the interview process, we want to hear your thoughts. Please approach interviews without the use of AI tools—our goal is to get to know how you think, solve problems, and communicate. Once you're in the seat, bring on the prompts!

    #32656. Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2343 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    Recent findings suggest that but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    According to recent reports, this sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    Recent findings suggest that so the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    In a recent development, one example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    According to recent reports, criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    According to recent reports, in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it states,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    It has been revealed that by now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Recent findings suggest that just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    According to recent reports, immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.
